newsitem.title: USA: Ex-tobacco executive fights Hong Kong extradition.
newsitem.headline: Ex-tobacco executive fights Hong Kong extradition.

text.p: A former Hong Kong tobacco executive who has spent 13 months in a U.S. prison fighting extradition to the British colony on bribery charges said he feared he would be executed if he were returned.

"You think I would get a fair trial in Hong Kong with my name and picture publicized in the case? They shoot people (in China) for ... a crime much smaller than mine," Jerry Lui Kin-hong told Reuters in a recent prison interview.

Hong Kong has charged Lui, a former export director with British-American Tobacco (Hong Kong) Ltd, with accepting bribes of $4.5 million in cash and loans from 1988 to 1993 as part of a scheme to smuggle cigarettes to China.

His controversial extradition case has become a test for Hong Kong's judicial system, which maintains it can give him a fair trial under Hong Kong law even after the colony reverts to China on July 1, 1997.
Under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong's legal system would be maintained after the handover to China. That includes the colony's recent decision to abolish capital punishment.

But Lui -- who maintained his innocence and claimed he was set up -- said he was worried about China's threat to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong and the frequent execution of prisoners in China.

Arrested at Boston's Logan airport in December 1995, Lui said he lost 15 pounds (6.8 kilograms) and almost suffered a nervous breakdown during his first few months in captivity. His family has been put under "tremendous pressure and pain," he said.

"I almost couldn't make it the first four months," he said in the interview at a Plymouth, Mass. corrections facility. "I had never been locked up anywhere in the world. I have been a responsible executive all my life."

In January, Lui won a legal round when U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro ruled he could not be returned because the United States has an extradition treaty with Hong Kong but not with China. Another hearing is scheduled for March.
The ruling undermined Hong Kong's campaign to convince the world that it would maintain its judicial independence after the handover. Hong Kong Gov. Chris Patton said he was "amazed" by the decision.
The United States government also issued a statement saying it disagreed with the U.S. court decision and it reaffirmed the extradition treaty with Hong Kong.
Hong Kong charged Lui took bribes and loans to ensure the sale and supply of cigarettes from BAT to Giant Island Ltd and other associated companies, which were then smuggled into China.
Lui said the primary evidence against him, a statement by Tommy Chui, a former executive with an export company, was full of errors.

"I suspect they have a hidden agenda behind my extradition, which is one of the major reasons why I have to fight," he said. "I have no confidence whatsoever in the Hong Kong government. This ... is a highly political case."
Lui admitted he received the money, but said it was part of a legitimate business venture to arrange the supply of Japanese, not British-American, cigarettes to Giant Island.
His U.S. lawyers said Lui passed a lie-detector test and claimed the facts from Chui's statement did not square with evidence of Lui's legitimate business transactions.
Lui has taken a keen interest in his own case, getting frequent reports from Hong Kong that are published on the Internet and relayed by his lawyer.
An MBA graduate from the University of Windsor in Canada and a millionaire from his 14 years in the tobacco business, Lui became a Canadian citizen two years ago.

He said he has not seen his family in Hong Kong since August, his legal bills have soared past $100,000 a month and his Philippine export business has declined about 60 percent during his incarceration.
The U.S. First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston has set a March 5 extradition hearing. The U.S. government is expected to argue that Lui should be returned to Hong Kong for trial.
